title: A review of "The Traveler"
gist: Santa Fe Institute professor Cris Moore reviews Andrea Wulf's new book The Traveler, about 18th-century naturalist George Forster, who sailed with James Cook at 17, entered the Royal Society at 22, publicly disputed Kant's racial theories, mentored Alexander von Humboldt, and died stateless and impoverished in Paris at 39 after leading the short-lived Mainz Republic. Moore reads Forster's life as a test case for the 'hopeful hypothesis of liberal science' — that open-minded observation of the world reliably produces respect for all forms of humanity.

insights.claim: The core premise of liberal science — that open-minded observation of the world inevitably produces love and respect for all its creatures and all forms of humanity — is presented as an unproven hypothesis whose validity is still undecided, not as an established fact.
insights.speaker: Cris Moore
insights.so_what: A reusable frame for evaluating whether more data and more exposure actually broaden institutional judgment, or merely rationalize existing positions — the same question that determines whether research-driven organizations self-correct.
insights.quote: that if we observe the world with an open mind, we will inevitably be drawn to a love for all the creatures in it, and all the forms of humanity upon it. Time will tell if that is true.
insights.locator: George Forster embodies the hopeful hypothesis

insights.claim: Forster's broad-minded recognition of dignity in every culture he encountered is characterized as rare in any historical era, including the present one — an explicit judgment that moral universalism has not become more common over 250 years.
insights.speaker: Cris Moore
insights.so_what: Signals the reviewer's implied view that openness is a scarce individual trait rather than a product of progress, which cuts against assumptions that cultural liberalization is a one-way ratchet.
insights.quote: His views would be rare in any age — including, sadly, our own
insights.locator: In her newest book, The Traveler

insights.claim: Forster combined empirical and emotional registers — described as observing 'with both his mind and his heart' — and deliberately learned the language, beliefs, and practices of the Maori, Tahitians, and Tongans rather than classifying them from a distance.
insights.speaker: Cris Moore
insights.so_what: A model for field research where immersion beats remote categorization — the analytic edge came from first-hand contact, not from theory imposed at home.
insights.quote: observed with both his mind and his heart

insights.claim: Forster's respect for Pacific societies was explicitly not relativism: he condemned the commodification of women and the coercion of islander women into sex with Europeans, and concluded that no culture holds a monopoly on good or evil.
insights.speaker: Cris Moore
insights.so_what: Shows a durable analytic stance — sympathetic observation paired with willingness to name defects — that is the opposite of both dismissal and uncritical advocacy.
insights.quote: great imperfections cannot be excluded from the best of human societies
insights.locator: Importantly, his respect for these cultures

insights.claim: When Europeans answered perceived theft or trespass with deadly violence during Cook's voyages, Forster inverted the framing and treated the islanders as the wronged party facing invaders, rejecting the prevailing 'savage' classification outright.
insights.speaker: Cris Moore
insights.so_what: An early documented case of an embedded observer contradicting the institutional narrative of the expedition funding him — the pattern to watch for wherever on-the-ground reporting diverges from sponsor framing.
insights.quote: Surely these people had a right to look on our men as a set of invaders

insights.claim: Forster's democratic politics are traced directly back to a field observation in Tahiti — that the lowest-status man spoke as freely to his king as to a peer — making anthropological data, not European theory, the origin of his egalitarianism.
insights.speaker: Cris Moore
insights.so_what: Illustrates how exposure to an alternative institutional arrangement reprices what a person believes is politically possible at home — the mechanism behind ideas traveling from periphery to center.
insights.quote: The lowest man in the nation speaks as freely with his king as with his equal.
insights.locator: Nevertheless, the structure of these societies

insights.claim: Forster rejected both poles of the era's debate at once, arguing that the contentment of the docile slave and the contentment of the 'free savage' are equally fictitious, and he publicly disputed Immanuel Kant's racial theories that justified slavery on grounds of European superiority.
insights.speaker: Cris Moore
insights.so_what: A reminder that the consensus intellectual authority of an era can be the one defending the indefensible, and that the dissenting minority position is sometimes the correct one.
insights.quote: The happiness of the tame slave is just as fictitious as the happiness of the free savage.
insights.locator: Wulf traces how this democratic instinct

insights.claim: Forster welcomed the occupying French army in Mainz as the instrument of liberty, became a leader of the Mainz Republic, and traveled to Paris to petition for annexation to France — arriving in the middle of the Reign of Terror.
insights.speaker: Cris Moore
insights.so_what: A case study in acting on conviction at exactly the wrong moment in a regime cycle: the ideals were vindicated long-term, the timing was fatal.
insights.locator: Near the end of his life

insights.claim: Forster first condemned the Terror as a 'court of blood' disgracing the revolution, then later rationalized it as the necessary price of the revolution's benefits — and the reviewer explicitly judges the first, instinctive reaction to be the truer one.
insights.speaker: Cris Moore
insights.so_what: The rationalization pattern — revising an accurate first reaction to stay loyal to a chosen side — is a reliable tell that judgment has been captured by commitment rather than evidence.
insights.quote: this court of blood is a disgrace of the revolution.
insights.locator: As Wulf carefully and movingly details

insights.claim: When Prussia and Austria retook Mainz, Forster lost his republic and his statehood simultaneously, was labeled a traitor by Germany, was abandoned by the intellectual and literary friends who had distanced themselves once he embraced the Revolution, and died in poverty and illness in Paris at 39.
insights.speaker: Cris Moore
insights.so_what: Reputational networks built in salons proved worthless the moment his position became politically costly — social capital priced at zero under regime stress.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the Prussians and Austrians had retaken Mainz

insights.claim: Forster's early trajectory was exceptionally fast — an expedition to Russia and the Kalmyk Steppe at age 10, Cook's Antarctic and Pacific voyages at 17, Royal Society membership at 22, and a well-received book, A Voyage Around the World — yet the rest of his career was marked by isolation and overwork.
insights.speaker: Cris Moore
insights.so_what: Early credential velocity did not convert into durable security — a caution against treating precocious accreditation as a proxy for long-run outcome.
insights.locator: On his return, Forster was made a member

insights.claim: Forster's decision to take posts in Vilnius and Mainz instead of Europe's cultural centers is named as a concrete cause of his stalled career, alongside loneliness, financial strain, and a marriage in which his egalitarian instinct to share his wife with other lovers broke down.
insights.speaker: Cris Moore
insights.so_what: Location relative to a field's dense center is treated as a first-order determinant of output and influence — network proximity compounds, peripheral posts do not.
insights.locator: Despite these heady beginnings and good connections

insights.claim: Forster's most durable return came through transmission rather than his own career: he traveled and wrote with the young Alexander von Humboldt, who later revered him as mentor and naturalist, and Wulf closes with an epilogue tracing Forster's lasting impact on science, literature, and politics.
insights.speaker: Cris Moore
insights.so_what: Influence realized through a successor rather than in one's own lifetime is a recurring payoff structure in research — value accrues to the network, not the originator's balance sheet.
insights.locator: Despite all this, Forster was incredibly productive

insights.claim: The Traveler, published by Penguin Random House and written by SFI Miller Scholar Andrea Wulf, was longlisted for the Baillie Gifford Prize for Non-Fiction on September 3, 2026, roughly a week before this review appeared.
insights.speaker: Cris Moore
insights.so_what: Prize longlisting is the standard demand signal for narrative non-fiction sales and rights; it also marks Wulf as a repeat producer of commercially viable science history.

insights.claim: Wulf's body of work follows a consistent and repeatable formula — biography-driven histories of 18th- and 19th-century science and philosophy, covering Humboldt's founding of biogeography, the wartime international campaign to observe the transit of Venus, and the German Romantics' quest for self-definition.
insights.speaker: Cris Moore
insights.so_what: A recognizable authorial franchise with a proven template is the kind of asset publishers and prize committees reward repeatedly — useful for predicting the reception of her next title.
insights.locator: Andrea Wulf is a historian, writer
